text: Severance is an American science fiction psychological thriller television series created by Dan Erickson and executive produced and primarily directed by Ben Stiller. It stars Adam Scott, Zach Cherry, Britt Lower, Tramell Tillman, Jen Tullock, Dichen Lachman, Michael Chernus, John Turturro, Christopher Walken, Patricia Arquette, and Sarah Bock. The series follows employees at Lumon Industries, a biotechnology corporation, who have undergone "severance"—a procedure that splits a person's memories between work and their personal life, creating two separate identities: the "innie," who has no knowledge of the outside world, and the "outie," who lives their life outside without knowing about their job. Erickson and Stiller first developed the series in 2015, with Apple TV+ greenlighting it in 2019, attaching Scott to the lead role. The first season cast was finalized by December 2020, and the second season cast was announced in October 2022. Principal photography took place in New York, New Jersey, and Newfoundland. The first season aired from February 18 to April 8, 2022, and the second season from January 17 to March 21, 2025. The series has been renewed for a third season. Severance has received critical acclaim for its cinematography, direction, production design, musical score, story, and performances, earning 41 Primetime Emmy Award nominations, including wins for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series (Britt Lower) and Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series (Tramell Tillman). Adam Scott received nominations for a Primetime Emmy Award, two Television Critics Association Awards, and a Golden Globe Award, while Stiller and Erickson earned Emmy nominations for directing and writing. Ben Stiller has an uncredited voice cameo as an animated version of Kier Eagan in season 1, and Keanu Reeves has an uncredited voice cameo as an animated Lumon building in a Lumon industrial film in season 2. Episodes in season 2 were promoted as being released on Fridays globally from January 17, but aired in American time zones on the preceding Thursday evenings. Erickson conceived the series during a period of depression while working an office job at a door factory after completing his master's degree in television writing, describing the job as monotonous and wishing he could "skip the eight hours of the workday, to disassociate and just get it over with." He submitted his pilot script to Ben Stiller's production company Red Hour Productions in 2015, which was passed to Stiller by Jackie Cohn and Nicholas Weinstock. Stiller read the script at least five years before the premiere and called it "the longest thing I've ever worked on," noting his enjoyment of its contributions to workplace comedy. Erickson described earlier versions of the pilot as "weirder" with elements like a disembodied pair of legs running by Mark, a charred floor with burnt desks, and a woman trapped in a glass cubicle, and credited Stiller with grounding the show by avoiding excessive surrealism. Stiller said he fell in love with the "weird human sadness" of a person willingly undergoing the procedure. In November 2019, Apple TV+ gave the series a series order with Stiller directing and Scott in the lead role. Stiller initially directed only the pilot but later directed more episodes. On April 6, 2022, Apple renewed the series for a second season. In April 2023, Beau Willimon was hired as an executive producer and writer for the second and potential third seasons. On March 21, 2025, shortly after the season 2 finale premiere, Apple announced a renewal for a third season. The Writers Guild of America West database lists Eli Jorne and Mary Laws as new showrunners for the third season, replacing Chris Black and Mark Friedman, who showran the first two seasons alongside Erickson. Media influences include the Backrooms creepypasta, The Stanley Parable (2013), Office Space, The Truman Show, Being John Malkovich, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, the Black Mirror episode "White Christmas," and Dilbert. Older influences include the existential hell in Jean-Paul Sartre's 1944 play No Exit and the totalitarian dystopia in George Orwell's 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four. Aesthetically, the series was influenced by Brazil, Dark City, and Playtime. Erickson's siblings inspired some characters. In 2016, his pilot screenplay appeared on Blood List's survey of the best unproduced genre screenplays. Erickson stated that the show was born from frustrations with workplace demands, noting that employees are expected to give endlessly with no meaningful return. In January 2017, Stiller invited Adam Scott to star; they had previously worked together in Stiller's 2013 film The Secret Life of Walter Mitty. Stiller intended to appear as a doctor in the first season but scrapped the role, saying it didn't feel right and that he's happy to be off-camera. In January 2020, Patricia Arquette, Britt Lower, Jen Tullock, and Zach Cherry were added to the cast; Tramell Tillman joined in February 2020, and John Turturro and Christopher Walken were added in November 2020. Dichen Lachman was cast in December 2020. Turturro recommended Walken for the role of Burt because he had known him for a long time and didn't need to act like friends. On October 31, 2022, Gwendoline Christie, Bob Balaban, Merritt Wever, Alia Shawkat, Robby Benson, Stefano Carannante, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, and John Noble joined the cast for season 2. Stiller offered former U.S. President Barack Obama a voice cameo in season 2, but he declined; the role went to Keanu Reeves. Production designer Jeremy Hindle blended corporate aesthetics from the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, citing modernist architect Eero Saarinen as influential for the building design. This included the John Deere World Headquarters in Moline, Illinois, and the Bell Labs Holmdel Complex in New Jersey, both designed as "work designed to do work," which served as both exterior and ground floor interiors for Lumon Industries. Set designs from Playtime also inspired internal sets. Main sets were created on soundstages in The Bronx: one soundstage featured around 140 feet (43 m) of hallway that was rearranged to create a maze-like structure, and another larger hallway was used in later episodes of season 1. A second soundstage was used for main rooms like the Macrodata Refinement Division, designed to create a feeling of being trapped with a large room (80 by 40 feet or 24 m × 12 m) and low ceiling. Hindle described this room as a playroom for new hires, with green carpeting to resemble grass. Other Lumon spaces were inspired by M.C. Escher. Erickson said the mix of cars and technologies from different eras was meant to "give a slight sense of disorientation" and make Lumon "feel unmoored from time and space." The production team sourced 400 anachronistic cars, mostly boxy 1980s and 1990s vehicles in good condition, each intentionally placed to create a retro science fiction aesthetic. Characters' vehicles include Mark's Volvo S90, Cobel's Volkswagen Rabbit, Helena's Lincoln Continental, and Milchick's Royal Enfield motorcycle. All office equipment carries Lumon branding. Prop designers reconstructed old computers with functional trackball devices so actors could perform the work shown, and the computers lack an escape key as a metaphor for the innies' lack of control. The terminals were modeled after 1970s Data General Dasher terminals, with keycaps recreated by Signature Plastics, who also made the original keycaps. The keycap set was re-released in 2025 under the name "SA Macrodata Refinement." The COVID-19 pandemic delayed the initial production start in March 2020. First season filming began in New York City under the working title Tumwater on November 8, 2020, with the opening scene shot on January 6, 2021. Filming occurred in Nyack, New York (for Mark and Cobel's homes), Kingston and Beacon, New York (in March), and moved to central New Jersey in April, primarily at the Bell Labs Holmdel Complex, which stood in for Lumon HQ. Filming was scheduled to conclude on June 23, 2021. Second season filming began on October 3, 2022, in New York City, with a planned wrap date of May 12, 2023. However, production was shut down on May 8, 2023, due to the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike. It resumed on May 13, 2023, in Newfoundland, was shut down again due to both strikes, and resumed on January 29, 2024, wrapping on April 23, 2024. In 2025, Severance became the most watched series in Apple TV+ history. Both seasons received critical acclaim: on Rotten Tomatoes, the overall series holds a 96% approval rating, with the first season at 97% (based on 117 reviews, average 8.5/10) and the second season at 94% (based on 223 reviews). The consensus for season 1 is: "Audacious, mysterious, and bringing fresh insight into the perils of corporate drudgery, Severance is the complete package." Metacritic gives the series an 85 out of 100, with season 1 at 83 and season 2 at 86, both indicating "universal acclaim." Reviews from Lucy Mangan (The Guardian) and Rachael Sigee (I) gave it five out of five stars, Huw Fullerton (Radio Times), John Nugent (Empire), Alan Sepinwall (Rolling Stone), and Anita Singh (The Telegraph) gave it four out of five, and Patrick Ryan (USA Today) gave it 3.5 out of 4. Mangan praised Stiller's direction, writing, and performances (especially Arquette, Turturro, Walken, and Tillman). Sigee praised the performances and called the series "original, weird, thought-provoking and beautifully crafted." Fullerton praised Scott's performance and called it "an impressive creation." Nugent praised the direction, performances of Scott, Arquette, Turturro, and Walken, and their chemistry. Sepinwall praised Stiller's direction, cast performances (notably Scott, Turturro, Walken, Lower, and Tillman), production design, tone, and season finale. Carly Lane (Collider) and Ben Travers (IndieWire) graded it an "A," with Travers noting the series "plays out cleanly and efficiently" and "knows how to make the most of its episodic format." Stephen Robinson (The A.V. Club) gave it an "A-" and praised Stiller's direction and the cast, highlighting Lower, Scott, Tillman, Turturro, Walken, Tullock, and Cherry. Kristen Baldwin (Entertainment Weekly) gave it a "B+" and highlighted Scott, Lower, and Tillman, calling Scott a "superb fit" and noting Lower's vulnerability and Tillman's charisma. Samantha Nelson (IGN) gave it a 9 out of 10, saying it sets up an intriguing mystery with room for character evolution. Shane Ryan (Paste) gave it an 8.1 out of 10, praising Scott, Arquette, and Tillman, as well as Stiller and McArdle's direction. Kyle Mullin (Under the Radar) gave it an 8 out of 10, calling it a "Golden Age of TV gem" and noting Stiller's strong direction in workplace scenes. The American Film Institute named it one of the ten best television programs of the year. The first season received The ReFrame Stamp for hiring people of underrepresented gender identities and of color. The second season has a 94% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with a consensus: "Masterfully managing its two halves of adroit character study and surreal nightmare, Severance's long-awaited sophomore season makes cognitive dissonance a mind-melting pleasure." Alison Herman (Variety) gave season 2 a perfect rating, noting it "fulfills this sine qua non with deceptive ease." John Nugent (Empire) gave season 2 four stars, saying it expands and deepens original mysteries while opening new ones. For its first season, the series received 7 major nominations at the 74th Primetime Emmy Awards and 7 additional nominations at the 74th Primetime Creative Arts Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Drama Series, Adam Scott for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series, John Turturro and Christopher Walken for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series, Patricia Arquette for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Drama Series, Ben Stiller for Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, and Dan Erickson for Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series.

The second season of Severance received a rating of 86 out of 100 based on 43 critics, indicating "universal acclaim." Writing for Variety, Alison Herman awarded the season a perfect rating, stating: "Season 2 fulfills this sine qua non with deceptive ease. Real-time viewers have had their patience strained; future binge-watchers will barely notice a blip." John Nugent of Empire gave the season 4 stars out of 5, noting: "After a storming Season One, Season Two expands and deepens the original mysteries while opening up new ones. Sharply made and skilfully executed, the employee benefits are there if you stay with it." The series received 10 major nominations for the 77th Primetime Emmy Awards and 17 additional nominations for the 77th Primetime Creative Arts Emmy Awards, making it the most-nominated series at both ceremonies. It won three acting awards: Britt Lower for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series, Tramell Tillman for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series, and Merritt Wever for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series, as well as five awards in technical categories. Notable nominations included Outstanding Drama Series, Adam Scott for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series, Zach Cherry and John Turturro for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series, Jessica Lee Gagné and Ben Stiller for Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, and Dan Erickson for Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series. The second season was teased during the Apple Event on September 7, 2022, which featured Helly (Britt Lower). The first footage from season 2 was released on June 10, 2024, as part of a promo for upcoming Apple TV+ programming. On July 9, 2024, a post on the Apple TV+ account on social media platform X teased an announcement about season 2, featuring a light blinking the word "tomorrow" in Morse code. The next day, on July 10, Apple TV+ announced that season 2 would debut on January 17, 2025. The first trailer for season 2 was released on October 23, 2024. On January 14, 2025, three days before the premiere, Apple TV+ recreated the show's 'Macrodata Refinement' office inside a glass box at Grand Central Terminal, where actors Scott, Cherry, Arquette, Lower, and Tillman entered and performed their roles for about two and a half hours, generating largely favorable public responses. On March 21, 2025, IKEA India and Australia posted the same advertisement promoting office supplies that replicated the Macrodata Refinement setup, using a tagline that pokes fun at the "mysterious and important work" joke made by office workers. On March 26, 2025, cast members Adam Scott, Britt Lower, Tramell Tillman, Zach Cherry, and Gwendoline Christie appeared at Tower Bridge in London to celebrate the renewal of season 3, with balloons featuring Adam Scott's face. On the same day, Apple updated its computer section on its website to include the Lumon Terminal Pro, which was not for sale but served as marketing to promote both the show and the Apple TV+ service. The official release dates of second-season episodes were on Fridays, but Apple TV+ released episodes the prior Thursday at 9:00 pm ET. The first season was released in the UK on Blu-ray and DVD on December 2, 2024, in Australia on December 4, 2024, and in the United States on December 17, 2024. An epistolary novel titled Severance: The Lexington Letter, released by Apple Books, purports to be a "tell-all" exposé of sinister occurrences at Lumon Corporation, presented as a dialogue between former Lumon employee Margeret "Peg" Kincaid and her innie (work self), sent as a letter to a Topeka newsletter. A fictional self-help book, The You You Are, was released by Apple Books as an e-book and audiobook, the latter read by actor Michael Chernus in his role as Ricken Hale. The official Severance podcast premiered in January 2025, hosted by Ben Stiller and Adam Scott, with each episode recapping a series episode and featuring interviews with an actor, crew member, or fan of the show.
